title: Conserved angular momentum lowers the corotation ratio in 0.1 to 0.2 solar-mass BHAC15 tracks
abstract: We test whether the contraction explanation of complex periodic variable (CPV) rates also predicts loss of CPVs along stellar spin paths. For fixed mass and rigid rotation, the corotation ratio changes as x2/x1 = h^(2/3) q^(1/3) u^(-2/3), where q is the radius ratio, h is the moment-of-inertia factor ratio, and u is angular momentum retention. In six fully convective BHAC15 tracks from 0.10 to 0.20 solar masses, conserved angular momentum lowers x by 19.4% to 19.9% from 20 to 150 Myr. The reported decreasing rate law then predicts a factor 4.09 to 4.26 increase if it remains valid along these paths. Angular momentum loss must exceed 27.7% to 28.4% just to make x increase. These are conditional model results, not measured torques, and do not reject the earlier fit at fixed period. Tracks that start at x = 3 end at periods of 0.091 to 0.113 days. The released survey has no selected 89 to 200 Myr rapid rotators below 0.15 days in its main colour range, so it cannot directly test this region. Exposed grey grains get 8% to 12% hotter along the same paths, but thermal crossing depends strongly on the assumed temperature limit. We provide an exact evolution test, aggregate coverage counts, sensitivity results, figures, original code, and input hashes. No new ages or light curves are added.

display.caption: The direction of change depends on spin evolution. From 20 to 150 Myr, conserved angular momentum lowers x, while fixed period raises x. The middle panel gives the angular momentum loss threshold for x to increase. The right panel shows periods for conserved-angular-momentum paths that start at x = 3. Six fully convective BHAC15 tracks span 0.10 to 0.20 solar masses. No torque is measured.

Analytic conditional rate changes for a fixed moment-of-inertia factor and f proportional to x^(-6.51). The zero-change line is J2/J1 = sqrt(R2/R1). The eightfold decline line is a benchmark, not a torque inferred from observations.

Grey grains get hotter along conserved-angular-momentum paths. The right panel shows initial corotation ratios that are cool enough at 20 Myr but exceed an assumed temperature limit at 150 Myr. These are model thresholds, not measured sublimation lifetimes.
